title: Data & Replication
text: Data & replication Evidence designed to be reused Historical data construction is part of the substantive contribution. Each public project documents coverage, source logic, transformations, and limitations so that the evidence can be inspected beyond a single regression table. Dataset 01 Monthly · Czechoslovakia · 1929–1938 Measuring Financial Stress under the Gold Standard A monthly dataset and composite index designed to recover the chronology of monetary, banking, and macro-financial pressure in interwar Czechoslovakia. 11 component indicators 107 monthly observations 1929:11 series begins 1938:09 series ends Research use identifying distinct phases of financial pressure; comparing market, monetary, and real-economy chronologies; evaluating conventional dates assigned to the Czechoslovak Depression; studying monetary defence before and after devaluation. Package contents underlying monthly indicators; transformed and standardised series; composite financial-stress measure; documentation and replication materials; transparent versioned DOI. Open dataset and documentation Dataset 02 Annual · Europe · 1927–1938 European bilateral trade, 1927–1938 Dataset: Commercial Hysteresis: Persistence and Reorganization in Europe’s Bilateral Trade Geography during the Great Depression. A bilateral panel for tracing persistence, destruction, and reorganisation in Europe’s commercial relationships across the Great Depression. 21 European economies 12 annual cross-sections 1927 pre-crisis benchmark 1938 late-interwar endpoint Research use separating aggregate trade collapse from link-level persistence; mapping partner substitution and regional reorientation; estimating intensive- and extensive-margin adjustment; studying the effects of exchange and clearing regimes. Unit of observation The core unit is the directional country-pair-year. That structure permits exporter, importer, pair, and time effects while preserving the geography of commercial adjustment. Open dataset · DOI 10.3886/E247132V2 Dataset 03 Monthly · Europe · 1925–1936 The Missing J The Missing J in Interwar Europe: A Monthly Cliometric Dataset on Effective Exchange Rates and Trade-Balance Adjustment, 1925–1936. Adam Dittrich · openICPSR · 2026 A monthly European dataset linking exports, imports, prices, economic activity, and exchange rates to the study of trade-balance adjustment. Annual bilateral trade weights drawn from League of Nations trade reports support the construction of effective exchange rates. Coverage Monthly observations for 1925–1936, with linked annual bilateral trade information. Variable availability and country coverage should be checked in the deposit documentation before building a particular estimation sample. Research use Comparing nominal and real effective exchange rates, tracing the timing of trade-balance responses, and distinguishing exchange-rate adjustment from changes in prices and economic activity. Open dataset · DOI 10.3886/E251239V1 In development Wider Czechoslovak data programme The public packages sit within a broader effort to consolidate scattered evidence on the interwar Czechoslovak economy. These components are under active construction and will be released only when their provenance and transformations are sufficiently documented. Building Monthly macro-financial database Central-bank balance sheets, currency and reserves, prices, industrial activity, labour-market indicators, trade, and bilateral exchange rates. Reconstructing Agricultural output and national income Crop quantities, livestock, prices, value added, and explicit assumptions for linking sectoral reconstruction to broader output estimates. Harmonising District-level Czechoslovakia Population, occupational structure, social and political indicators, and electoral outcomes for the 1920s and 1930s. Replication principles A dataset should expose its judgement calls Provenance Every series should be traceable to an archival table, statistical publication, or documented secondary reconstruction. Transformations Deflation, interpolation, seasonal adjustment, harmonisation, and index construction should be visible rather than buried. Uncertainty Alternative assumptions and fragile links belong in the package, not only in private working files. Versioning Stable repositories and versioned DOIs make it possible to distinguish a cited release from later improvements. Questions about Czechoslovak historical data? Discuss data or collaboration

title: Adam Dittrich, PhD
text: Economic historian · Prague Adam Dittrich , PhD Assistant Professor · Economic History Prague University of Economics and Business I study how monetary regimes, financial institutions, and economic ideas shaped adjustment in interwar Central Europe—especially Czechoslovakia. My work combines archival research, historical reconstruction, and cliometric methods. Explore research View publications Download CV Monetary history · Financial history · International trade · Historical measurement · History of economic thought 1920s–1930s core historical period Monthly + bilateral new historical evidence Archives + econometrics integrated research design Central Europe international questions Research agenda A small economy under large constraints Czechoslovakia provides unusually sharp evidence on the central dilemmas of the interwar economy: monetary credibility versus domestic recovery, financial stability versus deflation, and national policy autonomy within a fragmented international system. I use that case to address questions that travel beyond one country. 01 Monetary regimes How did gold-standard commitments, reserve rules, and central-bank strategy shape the timing and distribution of adjustment? Read the research theme → 02 Financial stress Can balance-sheet and market indicators recover the chronology of banking pressure before failures or institutional breaks become visible? Read the research theme → 03 Trade and adjustment How did devaluation, exchange controls, and changing relative prices affect trade adjustment during the Great Depression? Read the research theme → 04 Economic ideas How did theories of value, causality, and economic order enter practical debates over currency, crisis, and state intervention? title: Research
text: Research Institutions, evidence, and adjustment My work asks how interwar economies absorbed shocks when monetary rules, financial structures, political commitments, and inherited ideas constrained the available policy space. Czechoslovakia is the empirical centre; the questions are comparative. Research programme The projects are organised around a common proposition: economic adjustment is not a single price movement but an institutional process with a chronology, a distribution, and a political language . Exchange-rate commitments alter bank balance sheets and trade incentives. Statistical conventions shape what later historians identify as recovery. Economic theories define which costs policymakers recognise—and which they treat as unavoidable. I combine archival interpretation with new datasets, descriptive reconstruction, panel methods, event studies, synthetic controls, and time-series analysis. Quantification is used to discipline historical claims; institutional evidence is used to keep the quantities historically meaningful. 01 Monetary and central-banking history Monetary regimes and central banking Why did policymakers defend particular parities, and when did credibility become economically costly? This strand studies the Czechoslovak koruna, the National Bank of Czechoslovakia, reserve-cover constraints, sterilisation, and the transition from external discipline to managed adjustment. The central issue is not whether “sound money” was intrinsically right or wrong. It is how a monetary rule redistributed adjustment across output, employment, banks, exporters, debtors, and the state—and how long policymakers could sustain that distribution. Selected questions When did monetary defence cease to stabilise expectations and begin to delay recovery? How binding were statutory and informal reserve constraints before the 1934 devaluation? Did devaluation change trade volumes, relative prices, or merely the accounting expression of adjustment? How did central-bank balance-sheet policy interact with fiscal and commercial policy? 02 Measurement and chronology Financial stress and banking Historical crises are often dated by spectacular failures. Yet pressure can intensify earlier through reserve losses, currency demand, liquidity contraction, market segmentation, or deteriorating bank portfolios. My financial-stress work reconstructs this latent process from multiple monthly indicators. The objective is both substantive and methodological: to identify the sequence of stress under the gold standard without forcing a modern crisis template onto an interwar institutional system. Current project Measuring Financial Stress under the Gold Standard combines eleven indicators for Czechoslovakia from November 1929 to September 1938. The resulting chronology separates the initial external and monetary shock, the high-pressure phase, the later real-sector trough, and the regime change around devaluation. 03 International economic history Trade, devaluation, and commercial reorganisation The Great Depression did more than reduce aggregate trade. It altered clearing arrangements, exchange controls, bilateral bargaining power, and the relative importance of commercial partners. This strand moves from national trade totals to bilateral relationships. Selected questions Which trade links recovered after the aggregate collapse, and which disappeared permanently? Did currency depreciation redirect commerce toward particular partners or product groups? How did clearing agreements and discrimination reshape network centrality? Was the post-crisis European trade map a return to the 1920s or a new equilibrium? My exchange-rate research combines monthly trade balances, prices, economic activity, and effective exchange rates. The Missing J dataset makes these historical series available for comparative work on European adjustment in 1925–1936. 04 Historical national accounting Historical measurement and output reconstruction Interwar Czechoslovakia is central to debates about the Great Depression in Central Europe, yet its macroeconomic trajectory is still described through fragmentary annual estimates, industrial proxies, and series built for different purposes. My reconstruction work develops a more transparent evidential base. I am developing the Czechoslovak contribution to a comparative Central and Eastern European GDP-reconstruction project with Matthias Morys and Marcin Wroński. The programme begins with agricultural output and value added, then links sectoral production, prices, intermediate inputs, trade, labour, and monetary data. The aim is not a mechanically precise GDP number. It is an auditable account of what can be measured, what must be inferred, and how alternative assumptions change the chronology and depth of the downturn. 05 History of economic thought Economic thought as a policy institution My PhD, completed in September 2026, examined Czech apriorism and its influence on interpretations of Czechoslovak economic history. The dissertation focused particularly on Karel Engliš, Jan Loevenstein, František Weyr, and their critics. I continue this work through research on economic method, theories of crisis, and monetary policy. Rather than treating doctrine as a detached history of concepts, I ask how teleology, normativism, causal explanation, and theories of value structured policy argument. Economic thought mattered because it defined admissible evidence, legitimate ends, and the relationship between monetary order and social cost. This perspective also informs my quantitative work: categories such as “equilibrium,” “stability,” and “recovery” are never purely statistical. They carry institutional and intellectual histories. Approach Historical questions first; methods made explicit I use methods appropriate to the evidential structure of each question: archival source criticism, balance-sheet reconstruction, index construction, panel estimation, PPML, event studies, synthetic control, shift-share designs, and time-series diagnostics.
